description: Group of cool dudes and dudettes facing the unknown frontiers
summary:
AWERNASA is a health monitoring terminal for a crew living in a sealed lava tube on Mars, on the slope of Elysium Mons. On a mission that we planned there is no doctor, so astronauts have to spot health problems early and know what to do about them on their own.

Habitat sensors, medical tests and wearable bands with other devices, all feed one database. Our backend, MOTHER, checks every reading against NASA-STD-3001 limits and works out the state of each organ group. The tablet app shows the result on a 3D model built for each person's body: green is fine, yellow needs watching, red needs immediate attention. Every alert says what was measured, which limit it crossed and how to proceed.

The app also has a map of the base with CO2, oxygen, radiation and crew positions in the habitat, a mission calendar, a daily check-in and three cognitive tests (PVT, Go/No-Go, DSST) compared against each person's own baseline.

The mission data showcases a 600 sol active colonisation mission, with special events, health hazards and simulated crew ailments. The synthesised data is based on the data shared by NASA and other public space program data.
details:
AWERNASA is a health terminal for a crew of ten living in a sealed lava tube on the slope of Elysium Mons on Mars. On a mission like that the nearest doctor is on Earth, minutes of signal delay away, so the crew has to notice health problems early and deal with them on their own.

How it works. Habitat sensors (CO2, O2, radiation, temperature, water), wearable bands (heart rate, SpO2, sleep) and medical tests (blood work, cognitive tests) all write to one MariaDB database. Our backend, MOTHER, checks every value against NASA-STD-3001 limits and rolls the results up into organ groups. The tablet app shows each astronaut on a 3D model generated for their own body measurements: green is fine, yellow needs watching, red needs action. Tapping a body part shows the readings behind it. Every alert names the measurement, the limit it crossed and the next step, for example "left leg: blood flow at 25% of the other limbs, check this limb now". The app also has a map of the base with readings and crew positions per room, a mission calendar, a daily check-in and three cognitive tests (PVT, Go/No-Go, DSST), each compared with the person's own baseline rather than a population average.

Benefits and impact. Body, environment and mind sit on one screen, so nobody has to piece the picture together from separate systems. Alerts tell people what to do, what need immediate attention and first signs of possible issues. The same approach fits places on Earth where help is far away: Antarctic stations, submarines, remote research sites.

Tools. React, Vite and three.js (react-three-fiber) for the frontend; Python and FastAPI for MOTHER; MariaDB with Python ETL scripts for the data; Docker, GitHub Actions and Tailscale for deployment. The body models are based on the open Anny model with MakeHuman assets. Data comes from public sources (NASA OSDR Inspiration4, LSDA, NOAA space weather, the MMASH dataset) and from our own synthetic generators. We used an AI assistant (Claude) to help with literature research, documentation, code and demo data; the concept, design, UI and UX have been designed and tested by us, humans.

What makes it creative. We designed for a specific place, a lava tube with its own rooms, airlocks and natural radiation shielding, instead of a generic spacecraft. It represents a real possibility of a Mars Colony. Health is shown on your own body rather than in tables, and the interface looks like a habitat terminal, with switchable colour themes and an optional CRT effect.

Factors we considered. No reliable link to Earth, so the app keeps working on stored data when the backend is down. A touch tablet as the main device. Limits taken from NASA standards, with every source listed. Personal baselines instead of one-size-fits-all norms. Two languages, English and Polish. And honesty about the data: synthetic records are labelled, the crew is fictional, and the app is an educational demo, not a medical device.
